title: Meta Markets Cross-Border Bond Offering as Infrastructure Spending Erodes Free Cash Flow
subtitle: The social media giant is turning to global credit markets while its AI buildout outruns its internal cash flow.
summary: Meta is marketing at least $20 billion in dollar and euro debt as its annual infrastructure spend heads toward $145 billion. The borrowing highlights a growing divide between accelerating advertising revenue and the steep cash drain required to train next-generation artificial intelligence models.

bodyHtml:
Every evening, billions of people lie in bed scrolling through Instagram Reels, tapping WhatsApp messages, or checking Marketplace. Meta Platforms runs the world's most lucrative digital billboard network. About 3.64 billion people open one of its apps every day, and companies pay vast sums for the privilege of sliding into their feeds.

It is one of the simplest commercial engines in corporate history: advertising generated more than 97% of the company's $64.6 billion in revenue last quarter. Everything else, from smart glasses to virtual reality headsets, remains pocket change on the top line.

Now, the enterprise that once funded its entire empire out of its own daily receipts is asking global bond investors for help. Meta is marketing at least $20 billion of fresh debt across both dollar and European credit markets, marking its first attempt to issue euro-denominated paper. While the company's regulatory filings state that proceeds are earmarked for general corporate purposes, Wall Street understands the subtext. The business is burning through cash on artificial intelligence infrastructure faster than its ad auction can replenish it.

The mechanism behind the deal is simple math catching up with aggressive ambitions. Meta shelled out $34.91 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter alone, consuming 54% of its total revenue.

Because cash outlays for servers and data halls outpaced operational earnings, Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the quarter, down from a positive $10.63 billion a year earlier. It is not alone. Big Tech has turned the investment-grade debt market into an AI financing facility, with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Oracle collectively marketing tens of billions in paper within days.

Yet Meta's position looks fundamentally different from its peers. Think of Microsoft and Google as commercial developers constructing office towers that they immediately lease to thousands of outside corporate tenants. Meta is building an ultra-luxury private compound entirely for itself.

The company operates no public cloud platform to rent surplus chips out to external startups when internal workloads dip. Every single server cluster and fiber line must earn its keep directly through higher ad pricing or longer user engagement. Every dollar Meta spends on compute has to earn its payback through an ad impression, not a monthly cloud invoice.

The bull case rests on the sheer durability of that commercial machine. Advertising revenue jumped nearly 26% year-over-year last quarter, powered by a 14% increase in the average price per ad as automated recommendation models delivered better conversions. Backing out a one-time legal settlement with state attorneys general, underlying operating margins came in at 35.4%.

The company also still holds more than $82 billion in cash and marketable securities. With the equity trading near 17 times forward earnings after shedding roughly a fifth of its value from recent peaks, loyalists see a high-growth tech champion priced like an old-economy cyclical.

The short seller sees an ad business quietly taking on the risk profile of a levered utility. S&P recently revised Meta's AA- rating outlook to negative, forecasting cash flow deficits of $39 billion this year and $71 billion next year as hardware outlays and $355 billion in future lease commitments compound. Hardware decays rapidly on the balance sheet: net property, plant, and equipment has expanded past $253 billion, driving depreciation charges up 44% in just twelve months.

That non-cash charge will mechanically compress operating margins for years, regardless of how many ads people click. If Meta must fund multibillion-dollar deficits entirely with debt while credit spreads widen, its fortress balance sheet will steadily erode before the technology ever turns a net profit.

For the stock to stage a sustained re-rating, the market needs a concrete answer to the single question management declined to answer on its earnings call: when does the spending curve bend?

Meta nudged its 2026 capex forecast up to a range between $135 billion and $145 billion, but offered zero forward guidance for 2027. If infrastructure spending plateaus next year, free cash flow will violently snap back into positive territory, making the current valuation look like a clear bargain. If capital outlays step up once again, the equity will continue to struggle under the weight of an infrastructure budget that outgrows its core cash flow.

Investors will get their next definitive signal when Meta delivers its fourth-quarter results. Any initial budget framework for 2027 will determine whether this bond sale is a brief liquidity bridge or the start of a permanent borrowing habit.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in META. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
